title: Vigil held as SIU probes disabled man's death
article: A vigil marked the spot Monday night where Charlie McGillivary collapsed last week following a "physical interaction" with Toronto police officers.

The burly 45-year-old disabled man who could not speak as a result of a childhood accident was walking with his mother near Bloor and Christie Streets, when he ambled ahead, as he usually did. Mr. McGillivary collapsed as police were arresting him; he was transported to Toronto Western Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

The case is now in the hands of Ontario's Special Investigations Unit, a police watchdog agency that has been juggling a flurry of incidents involving civilians and police that have resulted in serious injury or death. The SIU is probing eight new cases since July 21. Three of the incidents - all in the last 8 days - have involved Toronto police.More than a hundred people gathered by Christie Pitts for Monday night's vigil, which allowed friends and neighbours to express their sadness and anger at Mr. McGillivary's death.
"We are going to have a moment of silence for Charlie, because Charlie was a man of silence," said Carly Steer, who lived in the same building as Mr. McGillivary and who organized the event.

Marlene MacDonald's mother also lived in the same building as Mr. McGillivary. She and her seven-year-old daughter Samantha knew him as a gentle giant, most often seen going on neighbourhood walks with his mother and helping out other tenants with groceries or other such things.
"I was sad," said Samantha, describing her reaction to the news.
Ed McKenna, 53, came to the vigil because he says this death in police custody, while not fully understood, is "not an isolated incident."

"As a taxpayer I'm fed up with hearing about citizens assaulted and murdered by police. I'm pro-union, but police shouldn't be hiding behind theirs. If I had done this, or if you had done this, we would have to answer for it. The police have no one to answer to."
In addition to the McGillivary case, the SIU is probing an incident early Sunday morning involving plainclothes officers and a man driving a Grand Am.

Jasbir Brar, a spokesperson for the SIU, said the driver refused to stop for police near Pharmacy and Conroy in Scarborough, lost control of the car and collided with bushes. Ms. Brar said a police officer fired at least one shot, striking Shane Maracle, the driver, who was treated at Scarborough General Hospital and released.

The SIU is also investigating the circumstances around the fatal shooting of 30-year-old Kevin Murray, allegedly armed and robbing people, at the Caribbean Carnival on the long weekend. Two bystanders were injured.

The conduct of officers in York Region is also being scrutinized, after Kaveh Sabouri Tabatabaei was shot to death in Thornhill last week, and, in a separate incident, a man suffered a non fatal gunshot wound when police were investigating a robbery in Aurora. And in Peel, the SIU is investigating the death of a man who was restrained on the ramp to Pearson International Airport's Terminal 3, and died in hospital.
Two fatal vehicle accidents - one in Morrisburg and the other in Hagersville - are also being probed.

While it may appear that there is a bump in SIU investigations this summer, experts caution against reading too much into the recent numbers. "Sometimes these things just tend to happen in bunches," said Professor Scot Wortley, a University of Toronto criminologist.
It serves to shine a light on the fraught relationship between the police and the civilian body charged with holding them to account.

Initially maligned by unions for criminalizing police work, the SIU has developed a "working relationship" with police services, even if questions remain over its ability to conduct investigations the way police can, said Prof. Wortley. An officer that is involved in the injury or death of a civilian has the right to refuse to talk to the SIU, in the same way that an individual can refuse to give a statement to police.

Critics argue that because police officers have the power to arrest and to use force, they should be forced to stand up and explain their actions. Friends and family of those killed or injured look at the numbers - that the vast majority of officers are cleared by the SIU - and surmise that the system favours the police.

"Sometime we feel the contrary," said Mike McCormack, president of the Toronto Police Association. "That [the SIU is] overzealous in their investigation. It's a matter of perspective. Our officers do a very difficult job in a difficult environment and it's part of the territory."

Tensions between Toronto police and the SIU reached new heights over the fallout of the G20, with public sparing between the Chief Bill Blair and SIU director Ian Scott, who has been openly critical of the level of police co-operation on some cases.

As of August 1, police in Ontario have to abide by new rules when they are the subject of an SIU investigation, as per recommendations from former Chief Justice Patrick LeSage. Officers who are being investigated must retain different lawyers than witness officers, which had not always been the case, and officers' notes about an incident must be completed at the end of a shift, instead of after speaking to a lawyer. Direct and indirect communication between officers is also explicitly forbidden until after the SIU investigation is complete.
